nodes.title: Filesystem: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Filesystem. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A sysadmin sets file permissions for an audit-logged shell script: OWNER must have full read+write+execute, GROUP must have read+execute (no write), OTHER must have read only (no execute, no write). The mode is written as a 3-digit octal. Which command sets the permissions correctly?
flashcards.back: Octal permissions: owner(rwx=7), group(r-x=5), others(r--=4) = 754. chmod 754 file sets this. Alternatively: chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r file. Use ls -l to verify.

flashcards.front: An XFS filesystem on `/dev/vg0/data` is currently mounted on `/mnt/data` via the command line. To survive a reboot, the mount must be PERSISTENT. Which configuration file should the admin edit, and what line?
flashcards.back: /etc/fstab format: device mountpoint filesystem options dump pass. defaults = rw,suid,dev,exec,auto,nouser,async. 0 0 = no dump, no fsck. After editing: mount -a to test without reboot. Use blkid to get UUID for more reliable mounting.

flashcards.front: A sysadmin needs to find EVERY file under `/var` owned by user `alice` (not group, but owner uid mapping to alice). Which command is correct?
flashcards.back: find /var -user alice: finds all files owned by alice. find /var -group devs: by group. find /var -perm /4000: find SUID files. find /var -mtime -7: modified in last 7 days. find /var -size +100M: files > 100MB. -exec rm {} \; to act on results.

flashcards.front: An XFS filesystem mounted at `/mnt/data` lives on an LV that was just extended by 10 GiB (`lvextend -L +10G vg0/data`). The filesystem itself still reports the old size. Which command grows the XFS to fill the LV?
flashcards.back: Expand LV: lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/data. Extend XFS: xfs_growfs /mnt/data (use mount point, not device). XFS can be grown while mounted. ext4: resize2fs /dev/vg0/data (use device). Always expand LV first, then filesystem.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.
